E049-01.notes: Colon correctly introduces the explanation of the flaw after an independent clause. B is a comma splice; C is a fused sentence; D 'which it tended' is ungrammatical (no role for 'which').

E049-02.notes: Sentence 4 lacks a main verb as written. A (nonrestrictive 'which' clause), B (participle), and C (restrictive 'that' clause) all leave 'Sundback's design' with no main verb, so each is a fragment. Only D supplies the finite verb 'used'.

E049-03.notes: A and B are dangling modifiers: the fastener did not increase the teeth. D still dangles and its inverted clause is awkward. C names Sundback as the subject of 'increasing'. Factually, Sundback did raise the tooth density (roughly 4 to about 10 per inch).

E049-04.notes: B is redundant ('thrill and excite'). C 'did a little' flips the meaning and clashes with sentence 8 ('did not catch on'). D is unidiomatic.

E049-05.notes: Two independent clauses with a cause-and-effect relation call for a comma plus 'so'. A has no comma before the coordinating conjunction, and 'and' loses the causal link. C 'although' sets up a false contrast. D misuses the semicolon before a participial phrase. A is the intended near-miss, not a second answer.

E049-06.notes: 'Few' is plural, so it takes 'know'. A and B use singular verbs; D is singular and the progressive form is unidiomatic. The intervening clause 'who use them every day' is the distractor.

flags.note: A is somewhat defensible. The essay does explain, in sentences 9-10, how the boots got the name 'Zippers' and how the name passed to the fastener, so a student could argue that the purpose is met. D is the better answer because only one of the four paragraphs is about the name; the other three cover invention, engineering, and modern use. Consider sharpening D's wording (e.g., 'only briefly explains the name's origin; it focuses mainly on...') so that the 'primary purpose' contrast is clearer.

E049-07.notes: B misstates the purpose (it is about mechanics, not the name). C is factually wrong because the essay does explain the word's origin. The choice is between A and D, and D wins because the name story is a minor part of the essay.

E049-08.notes: The sentence about farmers is off-topic in the naming paragraph. A claims a causal link the sentence does not make. B is false because the sentence is about boot wearers generally, not the first users of the fastener. D is wrong because nothing in it contradicts Goodrich. C's 'unrelated to the history of the fastener' fits.

fact_check: Judson's 1893 clasp-locker patents are accurate (granted in 1893). Sundback is accurate: Swedish-born, at Universal Fastener (which became Hookless Fastener Co.), Judson's successor company, with the design around 1913, so 'two decades later' works. 'Hookless fastener' is accurate (Hookless No. 2). Goodrich in 1923 is accurate: rubber galoshes branded 'Zipper', a name attributed to president Bertram Work and linked to the sound. Minor nonblocking notes: (1) Calling each tooth 'a tiny hook' sits oddly beside the 'hookless' name. Real Sundback teeth have a nib (projection) and a pocket, so 'a small bump' or 'a scoop' would be more accurate. (2) 'Did not catch on until 1923' simplifies the history: the fastener was already used on money belts and tobacco pouches, and clothing adoption came mostly in the 1930s. Neither affects any key.
